data.name: undo.nothingChanged

data.name: fix.dumpsAutomatic.explain
data.value: Sets the crash dump type to "Automatic memory dump" (Windows' default) so the next blue screen leaves a file that names the cause.

data.name: fix.preview.restorePoint
data.value: PC Doctor will first create a System Restore point and check that it exists. If it cannot, nothing is changed. Every change is recorded so you can undo it from the Changes tab.

data.name: journal.undoAll.confirm
data.value: Put back every change PC Doctor made, newest first? Settings that something else changed since will be left as they are and listed.

data.name: journal.restorePointNote
data.value: Undo puts back the exact old values. A System Restore point is the last resort: it also rolls back drivers, apps and updates installed after it.

data.name: journal.state.UndoConflict
data.value: Changed since by something else; not undone

data.name: settings.redact
data.value: Hide my user name and PC name in exported reports

data.name: settings.privacy.text
data.value: Everything PC Doctor does happens on this PC. It sends no telemetry. Network use is limited to features you start: Defender signature updates, the Microsoft symbol server, the Microsoft Safety Scanner download, optional VirusTotal hash lookups with your own key, and the optional update check.

data.name: m11.win10.why
data.value: Without security updates, newly found Windows vulnerabilities stay open on this PC unless it is enrolled in Extended Security Updates (ESU). PC Doctor cannot detect ESU enrolment.

data.name: m11.win10.action
data.value: Upgrade to Windows 11 if the PC supports it, or enrol in ESU. The ESU dates in the evidence change often; check Microsoft's page.

data.name: m11.av.defender
data.value: Microsoft Defender Antivirus is the active antivirus.

data.name: m11.av.thirdParty
data.value: Your active antivirus is {0}. Defender is in "{1}" mode, so a Defender scan is not available. Use {0} to scan.

data.name: m11.noAv.why
data.value: Defender is not running in normal mode and Windows Security Center lists no other enabled antivirus.

data.name: m11.noAv.action
data.value: Open Windows Security > Virus & threat protection and turn protection on, or check that your antivirus is running.

data.name: m11.rtp.why
data.value: Files are not checked when they are downloaded or opened.

data.name: m11.rtp.action
data.value: Turn it on in Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings. PC Doctor never changes Defender settings itself.

data.name: m11.tamper.why
data.value: Without it, malware running as administrator can turn Defender off.

data.name: m11.tamper.action
data.value: Turn it on in Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings.

data.name: m11.signatures.title
data.value: Defender security intelligence is {0} days old

data.name: m11.signatures.action
data.value: Run Windows Update or Windows Security > Protection updates > Check for updates.

data.name: m11.firewall.why
data.value: Programs on other devices in the network can reach services on this PC.

data.name: m11.firewall.action
data.value: Turn the firewall back on in Windows Security > Firewall & network protection, unless another firewall product manages it.

data.name: m11.uac.title
data.value: User Account Control is turned off

data.name: m11.uac.why
data.value: Every program you start runs with full administrator rights.

data.name: m11.uac.action
data.value: Set EnableLUA back to 1 (Control Panel > User Accounts > Change User Account Control settings) and restart.

data.name: m11.uacPrompt.title
data.value: Administrators are elevated without a prompt

data.name: m11.uacPrompt.why
data.value: Programs can gain administrator rights silently.

data.name: m11.uacPrompt.action
data.value: Move the User Account Control slider back to the default level.

data.name: m11.secureBoot.why
data.value: Malware that loads before Windows (bootkits) is not blocked.

data.name: m11.secureBoot.action
data.value: Turn Secure Boot on in the UEFI/BIOS settings. Check the PC maker's instructions first.

data.name: m11.secureBoot.legacy
data.value: No UEFI Secure Boot state: the PC may be booting in legacy BIOS mode.

data.name: m11.tpm.title
data.value: The TPM is missing, disabled or not activated

data.name: m11.tpm.why
data.value: BitLocker, Windows Hello and Windows 11 rely on the TPM.

data.name: m11.tpm.action
data.value: Enable the TPM (often called PTT or fTPM) in the UEFI/BIOS settings.

data.name: m11.bitlocker.title
data.value: The system drive is not encrypted

data.name: m11.bitlocker.why
data.value: If the PC is lost or stolen, its files can be read by removing the drive.

data.name: m11.bitlocker.action
data.value: Turn on BitLocker or Device Encryption in Settings, and store the recovery key somewhere safe.

data.name: m11.vbs.detail
data.value: Status {0} (0 off, 1 configured but not running, 2 running).

data.name: m11.hvci.why
data.value: Memory integrity stops malicious or vulnerable drivers from running kernel code. Some older drivers are incompatible, and it can cost some gaming performance.

data.name: m11.hvci.action
data.value: Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation lists the drivers that block it.

data.name: m11.sac.eval
data.value: Evaluation mode: Windows is deciding whether to turn it on.

data.name: m11.sac.off
data.value: Off. Turning it back on requires resetting or reinstalling Windows.

data.name: m11.lsa.why
data.value: Credential-stealing tools can read sign-in secrets from the LSA process more easily.

data.name: m11.lsa.action
data.value: Turn on Local Security Authority protection in Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation.

data.name: m11.smb1.title
data.value: The obsolete SMBv1 protocol is installed

data.name: m11.smb1.why
data.value: SMBv1 has no modern protections and was used by the WannaCry worm.

data.name: m11.smb1.action
data.value: Remove "SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support" in Windows Features, unless an old device you use needs it.

data.name: m11.rdp.nla
data.value: Remote Desktop is on, with Network Level Authentication.

data.name: m11.rdp.noNla
data.value: Remote Desktop is on without Network Level Authentication.

data.name: m11.rdp.title
data.value: Remote Desktop is on without Network Level Authentication

data.name: m11.rdp.why
data.value: Attackers can reach the Windows sign-in screen before proving who they are.

data.name: m11.rdp.action
data.value: Turn on "Require devices to use Network Level Authentication" in Settings > System > Remote Desktop, or turn Remote Desktop off.

data.name: m11.reboot.why
data.value: Some updates or changes are not finished until Windows restarts.

data.name: m11.lastUpdate.title
data.value: No Windows update installed in {0} days

data.name: m11.lastUpdate.why
data.value: Windows normally installs security updates every month.

data.name: m11.lastUpdate.action
data.value: Open Settings > Windows Update and check for updates. Look for an error code if it fails.

data.name: m5.check.events
data.value: Crash-related events in the System and Application logs

data.name: m5.check.events.detail
data.value: {0} events read from the last {1} days; {2} unexpected stops.

data.name: m5.check.suppressed.detail
data.value: {0} Kernel-PnP 219 events for WudfRd at startup were not reported: they are a harmless timing message.

data.name: m5.check.stability.none
data.value: Reliability data is not being collected on this PC.

data.name: m5.check.dumpAnalysis
data.value: Crash dump analysis with the Windows debugger

data.name: m5.dumpMode.none
data.value: Off: blue screens leave no dump file.

data.name: m5.dumpsDisabled.why
data.value: Without a dump file, the cause of the next blue screen cannot be identified.

data.name: m5.dumpsDisabled.action
data.value: Turn on automatic crash dumps (Windows' default). PC Doctor can do it for you, with undo.

data.name: m5.dumpsDisabled.undo
data.value: The old value is kept in the change journal and can be put back from the Changes tab.

data.name: m5.noPagefile.why
data.value: Windows writes crash dumps through the page file; without one, a blue screen may leave no dump.

data.name: m5.noPagefile.action
data.value: Set the page file back to "Automatically manage" in System Properties > Advanced > Performance > Virtual memory.

data.name: m5.dumpFailed.title
data.value: Windows could not save a crash dump ({0} times)

data.name: m5.dumpFailed.why
data.value: The crash happened, but the file that would explain it was not written (volmgr event 161).

data.name: m5.dumpFailed.action
data.value: Check that the page file is system-managed and the system drive has free space.

data.name: m5.check.dumps.none
data.value: No crash dump files on this PC.

data.name: m5.bsod.title
data.value: {0} of {1} blue screens in {2} days had stop code {3} ({4})

data.name: m5.bsod.why.unknown
data.value: PC Doctor's knowledge base has no explanation for this stop code yet.

data.name: m5.bsod.action.unknown
data.value: Look up the stop code in Microsoft's bug check reference.

data.name: m5.forcedOff.title
data.value: The PC was forced off while unresponsive ({0} times)

data.name: m5.forcedOff.why
data.value: Windows recorded that the power button was held down. That usually means the PC froze.

data.name: m5.forcedOff.action
data.value: Note what was running when it froze. Check graphics and storage drivers and temperatures.

data.name: m5.forcedOff.action.related
data.value: {0} related events (graphics or storage resets, hardware errors) happened just before. See the evidence.

data.name: m5.powerLoss.title
data.value: The PC stopped without shutting down ({0} times)

data.name: m5.powerLoss.why
data.value: There was no blue screen and no power-button press: power was lost or the PC hung hard.

data.name: m5.powerLoss.action
data.value: Check hardware errors below, the power supply and cabling, temperatures, and remove overclocks.

data.name: m5.powerLoss.action.related
data.value: {0} related events (graphics or storage resets, hardware errors) happened just before. See the evidence.

data.name: m5.wheaFatal.why
data.value: The processor or memory reported an error it could not correct (WHEA-Logger 18).

data.name: m5.wheaPcie.title
data.value: {0} corrected PCI Express errors from device {1}

data.name: m5.wheaPcie.why
data.value: Corrected errors are fixed by the hardware, but many of them can point to a loose card, a riser cable or link power saving problems.

data.name: m5.wheaPcie.action
data.value: Reseat the device, update chipset drivers and BIOS. The vendor and device IDs identify the device.

data.name: m5.wheaCorrected.why
data.value: The hardware fixed these itself, but they often precede uncorrectable errors on unstable overclocks or failing memory.

data.name: m5.tdr.title
data.value: The display driver stopped responding and recovered {0} times

data.name: m5.tdr.why
data.value: Windows reset the graphics driver (Display event 4101). Repeated resets can end in a freeze or blue screen.

data.name: m5.tdr.action
data.value: Install the current driver from the GPU maker, remove GPU overclocks and check GPU temperatures. Do not edit the TDR registry keys.

data.name: m5.firmwareLimit.title
data.value: Firmware limited the processor speed ({0} times)

data.name: m5.firmwareLimit.why
data.value: This is not a failure. It means the CPU was slowed, often because of heat or power limits (Kernel-Processor-Power 37).

data.name: m5.firmwareLimit.action
data.value: If the PC feels slow, check cooling and the power plan. On laptops this is common on battery.

data.name: m5.storage.disk7.title
data.value: The disk reported bad blocks ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.disk7.why
data.value: Part of the disk could not be read reliably. Data in those blocks may be lost.

data.name: m5.storage.disk11.title
data.value: The disk controller reported errors ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.disk11.why
data.value: Commands to the disk failed. Cables, ports, the controller driver or the disk itself can cause this.

data.name: m5.storage.disk51.title
data.value: Errors while paging to disk ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.disk51.why
data.value: Windows had trouble writing memory pages to disk, which can cause freezes and crashes.

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs55.why
data.value: NTFS found damaged file system structures. Files on that volume may be affected.

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs98.title
data.value: A volume needs a file system check ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs98.why
data.value: NTFS marked a volume as needing repair.

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs50.why
data.value: Data Windows had cached could not be written to disk, so some changes may be lost.

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs140.why
data.value: Often logged when a USB drive is removed without ejecting. Repeated on an internal disk, it can point to a storage problem.

data.name: m5.storage.storport129.title
data.value: The storage driver reset the disk ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.storport129.why
data.value: The disk stopped answering and was reset. This often comes before freezes.

data.name: m5.storage.storport153.why
data.value: Reads or writes timed out and were retried. Firmware, drivers, cables or a failing disk can cause this.

data.name: m5.storage.disk157.title
data.value: A disk was removed unexpectedly ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.disk157.why
data.value: Normal for USB drives pulled out without ejecting. For an internal disk it can mean a loose connection.

data.name: m5.storage.action
data.value: Check the disk health section, update storage drivers and SSD firmware, and check cables.

data.name: m5.storage.action.backup
data.value: Back up your files now, then check the disk health section and run a read-only disk check (chkdsk /scan).

data.name: m5.serviceCrash.why
data.value: A background service crashed. Windows may have restarted it, but whatever it provides was interrupted.

data.name: m5.serviceCrash.action
data.value: Update or reinstall the app the service belongs to.

data.name: m5.serviceStart.title
data.value: {0} services failed to start or timed out

data.name: m5.serviceStart.why
data.value: This is common on healthy PCs (for example, a service for a device that is not present). It matters only if something you use does not work.

data.name: m5.serviceStart.action
data.value: If a feature you use is broken, update or reinstall the app that owns the service named in the evidence.

data.name: m5.app.title
data.value: {0} crashed {1} times and stopped responding {2} times

data.name: m5.app.why
data.value: Repeated crashes of one app usually come from that app or a plug-in it loads, not from Windows.

data.name: m5.app.action
data.value: Update or reinstall the app. If the faulting module in the evidence belongs to another product, update that product.

data.name: m7.check.disks.none
data.value: Windows' storage management data could not be read.

data.name: m7.check.usbRaid.detail
data.value: Windows does not pass health data through most USB enclosures and RAID controllers. If smartctl is installed it can read them; PC Doctor does not ship it.

data.name: m7.health.healthy
data.value: Windows reports Healthy. This is the drive's own self-assessment, not a guarantee.

data.name: m7.unhealthy.title
data.value: Back up now: {0} reports it is failing

data.name: m7.unhealthy.why
data.value: The drive's own monitoring says it is degrading. Drives in this state can stop working without further warning.

data.name: m7.backupNow
data.value: Back up your files now. Then replace the drive or contact the PC maker.

data.name: m7.uncorrected.why
data.value: Uncorrected errors mean data could not be read or written correctly.

data.name: m7.latency.title
data.value: {0} took more than {1} seconds to answer at least once

data.name: m7.latency.why
data.value: Very slow responses cause freezes and can be an early sign of a failing drive or connection.

data.name: m7.latency.action
data.value: Update SSD firmware and storage drivers, check cables, and keep a current backup.

data.name: m7.wear.title
data.value: {0} has used {1}% of its rated endurance

data.name: m7.wear.why
data.value: SSDs wear with writes. Once the counter passes its rated maximum the drive is outside its rated life, though many keep working.

data.name: m7.wear.action
data.value: Keep backups current and plan a replacement.

data.name: m7.nvme.badLog
data.value: The drive returned a health log PC Doctor could not read.

data.name: m7.nvmeCritical.title
data.value: Back up now: {0} raised a critical warning ({1})

data.name: m7.nvmeCritical.why
data.value: The NVMe drive itself flagged a critical condition (spare space, temperature, reliability or read-only mode).

data.name: m7.nvmeMedia.title
data.value: {0} logged {1} media and data integrity errors

data.name: m7.nvmeMedia.why
data.value: The drive could not recover some data it stored. If this number grows, the drive is failing.

data.name: m7.nvmeTemp.why
data.value: Hot NVMe drives slow themselves down and wear faster.

data.name: m7.nvmeTemp.action
data.value: Improve airflow or add a heatsink to the drive.

data.name: m7.smart.title
data.value: Disk {0} reports reallocated or unreadable sectors

data.name: m7.smart.why
data.value: SMART attributes 5, 187, 197 and 198 count sectors the drive had to replace or could not read. Rising counts predict failure.

data.name: m9.check.devices
data.value: Devices with problems in Device Manager

data.name: m9.check.devices.detail
data.value: {0} devices with problems; {1} not connected or disabled by you (hidden).

data.name: m9.device.action
data.value: Open Device Manager, check the device's status, and install the driver from the device or PC maker.

data.name: m9.code.1
data.value: The device is not configured correctly (code 1).

data.name: m9.code.3
data.value: The driver may be damaged, or Windows is low on memory (code 3).

data.name: m9.code.12
data.value: The device cannot find enough free resources (code 12).

data.name: m9.code.14
data.value: The device needs a restart to work (code 14).

data.name: m9.code.18
data.value: The driver needs to be reinstalled (code 18).

data.name: m9.code.19
data.value: Windows cannot start the device because its registry configuration is damaged (code 19).

data.name: m9.code.24
data.value: The device is not present, not working, or missing drivers (code 24).

data.name: m9.code.39
data.value: The driver is corrupted or missing (code 39).

data.name: m9.code.43
data.value: Windows stopped the device because it reported problems (code 43).

data.name: m9.code.48
data.value: The driver was blocked because it has known problems (code 48).

data.name: m9.code.52
data.value: Windows cannot verify the driver's signature (code 52).

data.name: m9.unsigned.why
data.value: Windows normally requires signed drivers. Unsigned ones were installed with signing checks relaxed, and their origin cannot be verified.

data.name: m9.unsigned.action
data.value: Replace them with signed drivers from the device maker, or remove the device software if you do not use it.

data.name: m9.old.title
data.value: {0} third-party drivers are more than {1} years old

data.name: m9.old.why
data.value: Old drivers are not necessarily a problem. They are worth updating only if the device misbehaves or appears in crashes.

data.name: m9.old.action
data.value: If one of these devices causes trouble, check Windows Update and the device maker for a newer driver.

data.name: m9.winring0.title
data.value: Vulnerable WinRing0 driver installed by software in {0}

data.name: m9.winring0.why
data.value: WinRing0 (CVE-2020-14979) lets any program on the PC read and write hardware directly. Defender flags it as HackTool:Win32/Winring0.

data.name: m9.winring0.action
data.value: Update the monitoring or fan-control app in that folder to a version that no longer uses WinRing0, or uninstall it.

data.name: m9.check.crashStacks
data.value: Third-party drivers named in crash dumps

data.name: m10.check.reportFailed
data.value: powercfg could not produce a battery report.

data.name: m10.check.noDesign
data.value: The battery does not report its design capacity.

data.name: m10.check.detail
data.value: Holds {0} of {1} mWh as designed ({2}%); {3} charge cycles.

data.name: m10.worn.title
data.value: The battery holds {0}% of its original charge

data.name: m10.replace.title
data.value: The battery holds only {0}% of its original charge

data.name: m10.worn.why
data.value: Batteries lose capacity with age and charge cycles. The 80% and 60% thresholds are PC Doctor's rule of thumb, not a manufacturer limit.

data.name: m10.worn.action
data.value: Expect shorter battery life. No action is needed unless it no longer lasts long enough for you.

data.name: m10.replace.action
data.value: Consider replacing the battery through the PC maker or an authorized service.

data.name: page.crashes.subtitle
data.value: Blue screens, freezes and sudden power-offs from the last 30 days, with the driver Microsoft's debugger names when the dump files can be read.

data.name: crashes.empty
data.value: No crashes, freezes or hardware errors were recorded in the period checked.

data.name: crashes.deep.body
data.value: Dump files name the driver that crashed, but Windows only lets administrators read them. A Deep Scan reads them through PC Doctor's helper.

data.name: m5.check.dumpAnalysis.debugger
data.value: Windows debugger analysed {0} of {1} dump files.

data.name: m5.check.dumpAnalysis.offline
data.value: The Windows debugger is not installed. The stop code was read from {0} of {1} dump files without it.

data.name: m5.culprit.title
data.value: {0} of {1} blue screens in {2} days name {3} ({4}), stop codes {5}

data.name: m5.culprit.why.unknown
data.value: Microsoft's debugger found this driver on the crashing code path. PC Doctor does not know which product it belongs to; its file properties name the maker.

data.name: m5.culprit.action.unknown
data.value: Find which program or device installed {0} (its file properties show the maker), then update or remove it.

data.name: m5.culprit.core.title
data.value: {0} of {1} blue screens in {2} days stop inside Windows itself ({3})

data.name: m5.culprit.core.why
data.value: When the debugger can only name the Windows kernel, the real cause is usually elsewhere: a driver that corrupted memory earlier, unstable RAM, or an overclock.

data.name: m5.culprit.core.action
data.value: Remove overclocks, run the Windows Memory Diagnostic, and update recently changed drivers.

data.name: m5.needDebugger.title
data.value: Install the Windows debugger to name the driver behind these blue screens

data.name: m5.needDebugger.why
data.value: Without it PC Doctor can read the stop code from each dump but cannot tell which driver crashed. The module names listed are only what the dump contains, not a verdict.

data.name: m5.needDebugger.action
data.value: Install "Debugging Tools for Windows" from the Windows SDK installer (only that feature is needed), then run a Deep Scan again.

data.name: m5.liveKernelGpu.title
data.value: The graphics hardware hung and was reset {0} times (live kernel reports)

data.name: m5.timeline.dumpFailed
data.value: Crash dump could not be saved

data.name: settings.symbols
data.value: Let the Windows debugger download Microsoft's public symbols

data.name: settings.symbols.note
data.value: Makes crash analysis more precise. Only file names of Windows components are requested from msdl.microsoft.com, over HTTPS. Off by default.

data.name: page.overview.title
data.value: What's going on with this PC

data.name: page.overview.subtitle
data.value: PC Doctor reads what Windows already records and explains it in plain words. Nothing changes without your consent, and every change can be undone.

data.name: page.findings.subtitle
data.value: Only things worth acting on are listed. Each one says where it came from, how sure PC Doctor is, and what was not checked.

data.name: page.changes.subtitle
data.value: Everything PC Doctor changed on this PC, with the old values, so each change can be put back.

data.name: page.settings.subtitle
data.value: Language, look and privacy. PC Doctor sends nothing anywhere by default.

data.name: overview.scan.body
data.value: The Health Check is read-only and needs no administrator rights. The Deep Scan also reads disk counters, the TPM and BitLocker, and Windows will ask for permission.

data.name: overview.module.nothing
data.value: Nothing to act on in what was checked.

data.name: findings.empty.body
data.value: Run a Health Check from the Overview to see findings here.
